title: Incidence of running-related injuries per 1000 h of running in different types of runners: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Videbaek S, Bueno AM, Nielsen RO, Rasmussen S
population: 13 prospective cohort studies or RCTs in novice runners, recreational runners, ultra-marathon runners and track and field athletes (815 abstracts screened)
findings: 13 articles were included after screening 815 abstracts.
Incidence ranged from 2.5 (long-distance track and field athletes) to 33.0 (novice runners) injuries per 1000 h.
Weighted incidence 17.8 (95% CI 16.7-19.1) per 1000 h in novice runners and 7.7 (95% CI 6.9-8.7) in recreational runners.
13 original articles were included after screening 815 abstracts.
RRIs per 1000 h of running ranged from 2.5 (long-distance track and field athletes) to 33.0 (novice runners).
Weighted incidence was 17.8 per 1000 h (95% CI 16.7-19.1) in novice runners and 7.7 per 1000 h (95% CI 6.9-8.7) in recreational runners.

The authors concluded that novices seem to face a significantly greater risk of injury per 1000 h of running than recreational runners; heterogeneity in injury, runner-type and outcome definitions challenged comparison.
limitations: Heterogeneity in injury definitions, runner-type definitions and outcomes; ultra-marathon data are sparse; exposure-based rates only, no progression data.
implications: Novice runners carry about 2.3x the per-hour injury rate of recreational runners (17.8 vs 7.7), so a novice flag should select the most conservative defaults; the abstract gives no definition of novice, so the engine must define it.
Use for risk messaging baseline only; no numeric progression rule follows.

Treat a runner with no or little recent running history as high risk: apply the most conservative load-progression and recovery settings. The ratio of pooled rates is about 2.3 (17.8/7.7) per hour of exposure, a descriptive figure and not a causal hazard ratio.
Because risk is per hour of exposure, cap weekly running time (not just distance) in the first weeks and substitute walk time or cross-training for run time.
Use 17.8 and 7.7 per 1000 h as reference rates only when displaying or testing relative risk across athlete categories.

verification.notes: Crossref: Sports Med 45:1017-1026 (online May 2015). Abstract matched. Removed the researcher's '1 year of consistent running' novice cut-off (not in abstract).
